data.title: Object Storage
data.tagline: A cloud storage service specialized in whole objects like images, videos, and files, accessed by link
data.learningOutcome: You can explain how the cover file, article record, and object address relate in this example, and know that a storage design depends on project needs.
data.description: For an article cover, the image bytes are stored as a file object while the database stores the article title, ownership, and related object key or URL. The page reads the article record and requests the image by address; access may be permission-controlled or time-limited, so a URL is not necessarily permanent or public.

learning.assumes: You have seen image or file upload features, or heard of cloud storage.
learning.outcome: You can explain how the cover file, article record, and object address relate in this example, and know that a storage design depends on project needs.

distinctions.label: Database
distinctions.explanation: In this example, the database stores queryable article fields and file ownership while object storage holds the file. Some systems store file contents in a database; choose based on query, transaction, volume, and access needs.

distinctions.label: Browser storage
distinctions.explanation: Browser storage belongs to the current browser environment; object storage lives on a server or cloud service. Access by address still depends on permissions, network reachability, and URL lifetime.

explanation.title: Whole files go to object storage
explanation.text: In this example, images, videos, and attachments are stored as objects; the article record keeps a related object key or address, while access depends on the project's permission setup.

explanation.title: Structured text goes to the database
explanation.text: In this example, the database record holds queryable article fields such as title, author, and status along with the related object key; the page then requests the cover according to the project's access setup.

explanation.title: Storage split in this example
explanation.text: This example keeps article fields that need queries in the database and stores the cover file as an object. Other architectures should be chosen based on query, transaction, and file-access needs.

data.boundary: In this example, the article record stores ownership, status, and the related object key for business queries; file access still follows the project's access-control path. Other architectures may organize this data differently.

lessonPractice.title: An article list searches by title and loads cover images separately. How are the two stored in this example?

options.label: Store the cover as an object, and its title and key in an article record
options.feedback: Correct. In this example, the cover file goes to object storage while queryable fields and its object key go in the database record. Other designs may fit other needs; consider access, transactions, and file size.

options.label: Combine the cover bytes and title in the same database field
options.feedback: This would combine image bytes and the title in one field, unlike this example, which queries article fields and requests the cover separately. Some systems store file contents in a database; assess access, transactions, and volume rather than assuming file size alone decides performance.

options.label: Keep both in this browser for everyone to view
options.feedback: Local storage exists only on this device; it is gone after switching devices or clearing cache.

data.agentPrompt: For this article example, store the uploaded cover as an object and keep the title, ownership, status, and object key or address in the database record. Check the project's existing access-control design, then upload a cover and confirm it still displays after refresh.
